## Why Wind Forecasting in Finland? {background-color="#0d1b2a"}

::: {.incremental}
- 🌬️ **Finland's wind capacity exceeded 7 GW in 2024** — grid operators need accurate short-horizon forecasts to balance supply and demand
- 🗺️ **FMI operates ~50 weather stations** distributed across Finland, each collecting hourly wind speed, temperature, humidity, and pressure
- 🔒 **Station data can be commercially sensitive** — a centralised model that pools raw data is not always feasible
- 🤝 **Solution:** Federated Learning — stations collaborate by sharing *model parameters*, never raw observations
:::

::: notes
Open with the real-world motivation. Emphasise that Finland's grid depends on wind, and the data is there — the challenge is privacy. FL is the natural answer.
:::

## Local Learning Task {auto-animate=true}

Each station $i$ trains its **own** linear model:

$$\hat{y}^{(i)} = \bigl(\mathbf{w}^{(i)}\bigr)^\top \mathbf{x}$$

- **Label** $y = ws_{t+1}$: next-hour wind speed
- **Features** $\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^7$: six meteorological inputs + bias

::: notes
Introduce the per-node model before showing the full feature table on the next slide.
:::

---

## Local Learning Task {auto-animate=true}

Each station $i$ trains its **own** linear model:

$$\hat{y}^{(i)} = \bigl(\mathbf{w}^{(i)}\bigr)^\top \mathbf{x}$$

| # | Feature | Notation | Why |
|---|---------|----------|-----|
| 1–3 | Lagged wind speeds | $ws_{t-1}, ws_{t-2}, ws_{t-3}$ | Wind persists hour-to-hour |
| 4 | Temperature (lagged) | $ta_{t-1}$ | Thermal gradients drive wind |
| 5 | Relative humidity (lagged) | $rh_{t-1}$ | Proxy for weather systems |
| 6 | Pressure (lagged) | $pa_{t-1}$ | Pressure gradient → wind |
| 7 | Bias | $1$ | Station mean offset |

All features **and** labels are z-score normalised using training-set statistics only.

::: notes
The auto-animate smoothly adds the table. Emphasise that ALL features are lagged — no future information leaks into the input. The normalisation of labels is non-obvious; explain why on a question.
:::

---

## FL Network Design: Two Systems {background-color="#0a1628"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**System 1 — Geographic k-NN**

Connect each station to its $k=5$ nearest neighbours (haversine distance):

$$A_{ij}^{\text{geo}} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{d_{ij}^2}{\sigma^2}\right)$$

$\sigma^2$ = median pairwise squared distance

*Assumption: nearby stations share similar weather*
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**System 2 — Correlation k-NN**

Connect each station to its $k=5$ most correlated neighbours (Pearson on 2024 training wind speeds):

$$A_{ij}^{\text{corr}} = \max\!\left(0,\;\operatorname{corr}(ws_i, ws_j)\right)$$

*Captures meteorological similarity beyond proximity*
:::
:::

::: notes
Key design question of the project. The geographic graph is the intuitive baseline. The correlation graph is the novel contribution — it can link stations that are far apart but experience similar weather patterns (e.g. both coastal).
:::

    lats, lons = [], []

        lons += [stations.loc[station_names[i], "lon"],

## The GTVMin Objective

$$
\min_{\{\mathbf{w}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^n}
\underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n} L_i\!\left(\mathbf{w}^{(i)}\right)}_{\text{local fit}}
\;+\;
\alpha \underbrace{\sum_{\{i,j\}\in\mathcal{E}} A_{ij}\,\bigl\|\mathbf{w}^{(i)} - \mathbf{w}^{(j)}\bigr\|^2}_{\text{graph total variation}}
$$

::: {.fragment}
| $\alpha$ | Behaviour |
|----------|-----------|
| $0$ | Stations learn **independently** — pure local models |
| $\to\infty$ | All stations converge to a **single shared model** |
| intermediate | **Personalised** — local fit balanced against neighbour agreement |
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
**Variation measure**: squared $\ell_2$ norm — convex and differentiable, making the full objective tractable for gradient-based optimisation.
:::
:::

::: notes
Build up the equation in two fragments. The table makes the role of alpha very clear. The callout justifies the choice of squared L2 norm over e.g. L1.
:::

---

## FedGD: The Algorithm

**Synchronous Federated Gradient Descent** — each iteration, every node $i$ computes:

$$\mathbf{w}^{(i,t+1)} = \mathbf{w}^{(i,t)} - \eta \Bigl[
  \underbrace{\nabla L_i\!\left(\mathbf{w}^{(i,t)}\right)}_{\text{local gradient}}
  + 2\alpha \!\!\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}(i)} \!\! A_{ij}\underbrace{\left(\mathbf{w}^{(i,t)} - \mathbf{w}^{(j,t)}\right)}_{\text{pull toward neighbour}}
\Bigr]$$

```python
# For each node i at iteration t:
grad_local   = (2/n_i) * X_i.T @ (X_i @ w_i - y_i)        # ← local MSE gradient
grad_penalty = 2 * alpha * sum(A[i,j] * (w_i - w_j)        # ← graph penalty
                               for j in neighbours[i])
w_i_new      = w_i - lr * (grad_local + grad_penalty)       # ← simultaneous update
```

::: {.fragment}
- 📡 **Communication per iteration:** $2|\mathcal{E}|$ messages (each edge, both directions)
- 🔒 **Raw data $\mathcal{D}^{(i)}$ never leaves node $i$**
:::

::: notes
The code block maps directly to the math. Stress that all nodes read current weights and update simultaneously — no sequential passing, no averaging. The privacy guarantee is immediate: only w vectors travel over edges.
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
Both systems select **$\alpha^* = 0.1$** — moderate regularisation balances local fit and collaboration.
:::
:::

::: notes
The log x-axis is important: alpha=0 is local-only. The sweet spot is at 0.1 for both systems. At large alpha, models over-smooth and validation loss rises again.
:::

## Convergence

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="65%"}
```{python}
#| label: convergence-slide
if results_available:
    iters = np.arange(1, len(geo_r["val_loss"]) + 1)
    fig = go.Figure()
    for label, arr, colour in [
        ("Baseline (α=0)",  base_r["val_loss"],  "#888"),
        (f"System 1 — Geo (α={float(geo_r['alpha']):.2f})",  geo_r["val_loss"],  "#4a9edd"),
        (f"System 2 — Corr (α={float(corr_r['alpha']):.2f})", corr_r["val_loss"], "#f97316"),
    ]:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=iters, y=arr, mode="lines", name=label,
                                 line=dict(color=colour, width=2)))
    for r, colour in [(base_r, "#888"), (geo_r, "#4a9edd"), (corr_r, "#f97316")]:
        rmse = float(np.sqrt(float(r["test_loss"]) * mean_y_std**2))
        fig.add_hline(y=float(r["test_loss"]),
                      line=dict(color=colour, dash="dot", width=1),
                      annotation_text=f"{rmse:.3f} m/s",
                      annotation_font_color=colour, annotation_position="right")
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Iteration", color="#e8edf2", gridcolor="#1e3a5f")
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Val MSE", color="#e8edf2", gridcolor="#1e3a5f")
    fig.update_layout(
        height=400, paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", plot_bgcolor="#111e2d",
        font_color="#e8edf2",
        legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.28, font_size=12),
        margin=dict(t=5, b=80, l=5, r=90),
    )
    show(fig)
```

::: {.column width="35%"}

:::

:::

The dotted horizontal lines show the final test performance in m/s — the unit that matters operationally. Convergence looks fast but the problem is well-conditioned (linear + convex).

## Per-Node Test MSE

```{python}
#| label: boxplot-slide
if results_available:
    from fedgd import _mse

    def _load_weights(r):
        w = r["weights"]
        return w.item() if w.ndim == 0 else {}

    geo_w  = _load_weights(geo_r)
    corr_w = _load_weights(corr_r)
    base_w = _load_weights(base_r)

    rows = []
    for node in sorted(datasets.keys()):
        X_t, y_t = datasets[node]["X_test"], datasets[node]["y_test"]
        rows.append({
            "Baseline":        _mse(X_t, y_t, base_w[node]) if node in base_w  else np.nan,
            "System 1 — Geo":  _mse(X_t, y_t, geo_w[node])  if node in geo_w   else np.nan,
            "System 2 — Corr": _mse(X_t, y_t, corr_w[node]) if node in corr_w  else np.nan,
        })
    ndf = pd.DataFrame(rows)

    fig = go.Figure()
    for col, colour in [("Baseline","#888"), ("System 1 — Geo","#4a9edd"), ("System 2 — Corr","#f97316")]:
        fig.add_trace(go.Box(
            y=ndf[col].dropna(), name=col,
            marker_color=colour, boxmean=True,
            line_color=colour,
        ))
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Test MSE (normalised)", color="#e8edf2", gridcolor="#1e3a5f")
    fig.update_layout(
        height=430, paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", plot_bgcolor="#111e2d",
        font_color="#e8edf2", margin=dict(t=10, b=10, l=10, r=10),
        showlegend=False,
    )
    show(fig)
```

::: notes
Hover over any box to see quartiles. The spread is large — some stations benefit much more than others. Sparse stations (northern Finland) typically gain the most from federation.
:::

## Prediction Quality

```{python}
#| label: pred-scatter-slide
if results_available:
    sample_nodes = sorted(datasets.keys())[:3]
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=len(sample_nodes),
                        subplot_titles=sample_nodes)
    for col_idx, node in enumerate(sample_nodes, start=1):
        X_test = datasets[node]["X_test"]
        y_test = datasets[node]["y_test"]
        y_pred = X_test @ geo_w[node]
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=y_test, y=y_pred, mode="markers",
            marker=dict(size=3, color="#4a9edd", opacity=0.5),
            showlegend=False,
        ), row=1, col=col_idx)
        max_val = float(max(y_test.max(), y_pred.max())) * 1.05
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=[0, max_val], y=[0, max_val], mode="lines",
            line=dict(color="#f97316", dash="dash", width=1.5),
            name="Ideal" if col_idx == 1 else None,
            showlegend=(col_idx == 1),
        ), row=1, col=col_idx)
    fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Actual (norm.)", color="#e8edf2", gridcolor="#1e3a5f")
    fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Predicted (norm.)", color="#e8edf2", gridcolor="#1e3a5f", col=1)
    fig.update_layout(
        height=420, paper_bgcolor="rgba(0,0,0,0)", plot_bgcolor="#111e2d",
        font_color="#e8edf2", margin=dict(t=40, b=10, l=10, r=10),
    )
    show(fig)
```

Points clustering near the **orange diagonal** indicate accurate predictions — System 1 (Geographic) shown.

::: notes
Three representative stations. Good stations cluster tightly on the diagonal. Weaker stations show more scatter, typically at extreme wind speeds where training data is sparse.
:::

## Conclusion

::: {.incremental}
- ✅ **Both FL systems beat local-only training** — graph regularisation enables meaningful collaboration across Finnish weather stations
- ✅ **Correlation-based graph ≥ geographic graph** — capturing meteorological similarity beyond proximity adds predictive value
- ⚠️ **Limitations:** linear model capacity, static graph (fixed before training), single learning rate for all stations
- 🔭 **Future work:** nonlinear local models (e.g. MLP), adaptive or time-varying graph construction, heterogeneous step sizes
:::

::: notes
Keep this slide brief. The incremental list builds naturally toward the limitations and future work — which is what reviewers and TAs look for in a course project.
:::
